findings.gate_said: The Time article at time.com/7309274 is dated March 11, 2026, not 13 August 2025. Additionally, the article quotes Tucker on automation bias but does not appear to quote Professor Osmani on procedure volume — Osmani's comments on the rise in colonoscopy volume appear in the Science Media Centre expert reaction page (sciencemediacentre.org), not in the Time article.
findings.why: The gate returned 'March 11, 2026' for the Time article and said it does not quote Osmani on procedure volume. Both halves are refuted by the bytes we hold. S040 carries this dateline verbatim, carries 'by Miranda Jeyaretnam', and carries Osmani to SMC on the rising colonoscopy count: 'The increased workload, Osmani suggested, could have led to clinician fatigue and poorer detection rates.' The gate has returned the same wrong date across three runs; it is reading a later metadata timestamp, not the dateline. This row exists so a fourth run does not spend money re-deriving it.

findings.gate_said: The draft says 'Nothing false was printed' about Fortune's coverage, but Fortune's article mischaracterises the study design by saying the drop occurred after the AI was taken away, when the study actually measured performance during AI use on the days without it.
findings.quote: after they no longer had access to the AI tools they were introduced to
findings.why: UPHELD. The objection's factual premise is true and is verbatim in S023's held bytes: Fortune describes the fall as occurring after the AI was removed, when the study measured non-AI days during a period of AI use. The attacked sentence is no longer on the page; the page now quotes this Fortune sentence, states that neither half of it describes the study, and records the reversal in its own text. Settled because the claim was wrong and the page no longer makes it -- NOT on the ground that the text moved. Whether the revision was made in response to this finding is not established from the bytes and is not claimed here.

The draft treats the letter as unread when its abstract, which contains the sentence in
findings.why: The finding asserts the Levartovsky and Kopylov abstract is publicly visible and describes a decline 'after computer-aided detection introduction and subsequent removal'. It is not reachable. Europe PMC's core record for DOI 10.1016/S2468-1253(25)00289-4 (PMID 41205615) carries no abstractText; PubMed shows no abstract; thelancet.com returns 403 and ScienceDirect is robots-disallowed; an exact-phrase search for the quoted sentence returns zero results. A gate's quotation of a document neither party can open is not evidence, and this is the more dangerous direction than a missing source, because the quotation was plausible and would have flattered the page's thesis. Closed as a judgement rather than against a document because an absence cannot be quoted. The page already names every route tried and asks readers who can open it to write.

findings.gate_said: Fortune carried the six-point fall to a business readership on 26 August 2025, connected it to an automation analogy and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study, and reported none of the eleven limitations.
findings.quote: The increased workload, Osmani suggested, could have led to clinician fatigue and poorer detection rates.
findings.why: UPHELD. The counterexample concedes the Fortune sentence is accurate for Fortune. What it attacked was Fortune standing as the lead instance of a GENERAL failure, immediately after 'none of it crossed the boundary'. That framing is gone with cov-3's sentence. The Fortune sentence itself survives in revised form -- 'automation analogy' is now 'aviation analogy' -- which is why a containment test on the gate's wording reads PARTIAL rather than PRESENT.

NOTE ON THE GATE'S OWN WORDING: it calls this 'the volume confounder' and 'volume doubling'. S040 contains neither 'volume' nor 'doubled' -- it says the total number 'increased'. The substance holds; the magnitude is the gate's gloss on its own rendition, not Time's words.
